name: Caranthir

claims.text:
Physically, Caranthir was notable for two characteristics: his exceptionally dark hair (inherited from his father's side) and his ruddy complexion (inherited from his mother's side). These became the bases of his father-name and mother-name respectively.
Caranthir's personality was noted as being harsh, haughty, and quick to anger. His words to Angrod not only diminished the standing of the House of Fëanor at the early council of the Noldor, but remained with Angrod, and the bitterness of them contributed to his confessing the deeds of the Noldor to Thingol many years later.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §104

claims.text: Caranthir is the Sindarized form of Carnistir, being a compound of caran (“red”) and þir ("face").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "From The Shibboleth of Fëanor" (edited by Carl F. Hostetter), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 41, July 2000, p. 10

claims.text: In , the first Men in Beleriand were encountered in Ossiriand by Finrod. As the Green-elves of that region were troubled by them, Finrod persuaded them to carry onward, and they settled in Estolad. Soon after, in , a second group of Men, the Haladin, arrived and, after they met the unfriendship of the Green-elves, they turned north and settled in Thargelion where the people of Caranthir paid little heed to them.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Two. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Coming of Men into the West (Chapter 14)", p. §13

claims.text: At this Angrod became exceedingly wroth and left the council. And though Maedhros rebuked Caranthir, his words troubled the hearts of the Noldor, who feared that the sons of Fëanor would ever be like to burst forth in rash word or violence. Thus, when it came to selecting an overlord of the Exiles, all save few chose Fingolfin. Maedhros then subsequently waived his claim to the title, and shortly after relocated the House of Fëanor to East Beleriand.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §§65-69

claims.text: The people of Caranthir took the easternmost area which lay between the river Gelion and the Blue Mountains and fortified the mountains east of Maglor's Gap. In the valley between Mount Rerir and the Blue Mountains, shadowed by them in all directions save the south, lay Lake Helevorn, and it was here that Caranthir had his abode. On the western slope of Mount Rerir itself was constructed a fortress.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §118; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §142

claims.text: The Sindar had previously called this area Talath Rhúnen ("East Vale"), however the Noldor referred to it as Thargelion ("(Land) beyond Gelion") or Dor Caranthir ("Land of Caranthir").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §118

claims.text: In about the people of Caranthir first climbed the Blue Mountains and gazed eastward unto Eriador, which to them seemed wide and wild. They soon after made contact with the Dwarves of the Blue Mountains, who had ceased their traffic into Beleriand since the onslaught of Morgoth and the coming of the Noldor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §114
claims.section: section == History == > Interaction with the Dwarves

claims.text: There was little love between them, for the Dwarves were secretive and quick to resentment, and Caranthir was haughty and scarce concealed his scorn for their unlovely appearance, and his people followed their lord. Yet, as they both feared and hated Morgoth, alliance was made and from it both had great profit. The smiths and masons of the Dwarves learned many secrets of craft from the Noldor, making them renowned among their kin, while the Noldor obtained great wealth of iron and their armouries became filled with weapons and harness of war. Further, until the power of Maedhros was overthrown, all Dwarven traffic first passed through the hands of Caranthir, and from this he won great riches.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §114
claims.section: section == History == > Interaction with the Dwarves

claims.text: Due to Caranthir's friendship with the Dwarves of Belegost, Eöl in turn much more often visited Nogrod.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: III. Maeglin"
claims.section: section == History == > Interaction with the Dwarves

claims.text: After the battle, the power of the sons of Fëanor was broken. Their realms and fortresses in East Beleriand were taken and garrisoned by Orcs, and they retreated to into the woods.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §242
claims.section: section == History == > Last deeds in Beleriand

claims.text: In , he perished along with his brothers Celegorm and Curufin during the Second Kinslaying, the attack by the sons of Fëanor on Menegroth in an attempt to recover a Silmaril from King Dior Eluchíl of Doriath.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"
claims.section: section == History == > Last deeds in Beleriand

claims.text: Caranthir was a Noldorin prince, one of the seven sons of Fëanor and Nerdanel, born in Valinor during the Time of the Two Trees. His appearance was notable, being as black-haired as of his grandfather Finwë, but having the ruddy complexion of his mother. At some point he married, but nothing of his wife or their family is known.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of the Sons of Fëanor"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes"

claims.text: Fëanor and his sons abode seldom in one place for long, but travelled far and wide upon the confines of Valinor, going even to the borders of the Dark and the cold shores of the Outer Sea, seeking the unknown. Often they were guests in the halls of Aulë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"

claims.text: During the unrest of the Noldor and the strife between Fëanor and his half-brother Fingolfin, Fëanor was banished from Tirion and took up residence in Formenos; he was followed by his father, King Finwë, and his sons.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Silmarils and the Unrest of the Noldor"

claims.text: They then sped to the Ring of Doom where Maedhros informed Manwë and, unknowingly, also Fëanor who kept himself hidden during the conversation. Fëanor reacted by cursing both Melkor and the summons of Manwë, and then fleeing into the night; the sons of Fëanor followed him, dismayed that he might slay himself.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Of the Rape of the Silmarils", §§7-12

claims.text: After a long march northwards, the Noldor drew close to the Helcaraxë, a land bridge deemed impassable, and the narrow strait between Aman and Middle-earth they intended to sail. With too few ships remaining to ferry all the Noldor at once, and the fear of treachery between their houses, Fëanor and his sons stole away in them, abandoning the host of Fingolfin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Flight of the Noldor"

claims.text: After landing at the Firth of Drengist, and burning the ships to prevent any from sailing back, Fëanor's host traveled north and encamped on the northern shore of Lake Mithrim where they were attacked unaware by a host of Morgoth. In the battle that followed, Fëanor's forces were swiftly victorious, and pursued the routed orcs over the Mountains of Shadow into Ard-galen.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Return of the Noldor"

claims.text: Though Morgoth's assaulting forces were destroyed, Fëanor recklessly drew far ahead of his host in pursuit of the remnant orcs, and was ambushed and mortally wounded at the confines of Dor Daedeloth. He was rescued by his sons, and just before his death he laid it on them to uphold their oath and to avenge him. Shortly after, Maedhros was taken captive after feigning to treat with Morgoth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Return of the Noldor"

claims.text: The host of Fëanor remained at northern shore of Lake Mithrim until the arrival of Fingolfin's host, having successfully crossed the Helcaraxë, with the first sunrise in . To avoid open hostilities with Fingolfin's larger forces, the remaining sons of Fëanor relocated to the southern shore of Lake Mithrim. The hatred between the houses began to be assuaged in , when Maedhros was rescued by Fingolfin's son Fingon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §59; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §61

claims.text: In , Morgoth broke the Siege of Angband with a massive assault against the Noldor. The Orcs broke through the Pass of Aglon and, led by the dragon Glaurung, breached Maglor's Gap. They took the fortress upon the west slopes of Mount Rerir, ravaged all Thargelion, defiled Lake Helevorn and came far into East Beleriand. Caranthir fled and joined the remnant of his people to the scattered folk of Amrod and Amras. They then retreated to the south and established a watch and some strength of war upon Amon Ereb where they had aid of the Green-elves.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §148; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §142

claims.text: But the Orcs came not into Ossiriand or South Beleriand. At some point prior to , Morgoth's army in East Beleriand was broken by Thingol on the borders of Doriath. Part had fled away south never to return to him, part retreated north and was stricken by Maedhros, and those that ventured near the mountains were hunted by the Dwarves.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §142; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §170

claims.text: In Swarthy Men came out of Eriador, passing north of the Blue Mountains, and entered into Lothlann. They were not unexpected, as Maedhros had been warned by the Dwarves of their coming from out of the further East. They were not a unified people, having many houses with little love among them. But Maedhros, seeing the weakness of the Elves and Edain, and the seemingly inexhaustible store of Angband, made alliance with them and gave them dwellings. Among these Men, the two chieftains with the greatest followings were Bór and Ulfang. While Bór swore loyalty to Maedhros and Maglor, and was presumably given lands within Lothlann, the folk of Ulfang were given lands within Thargelion, and he and his sons, Uldor, Ulfast, and Ulwarth, swore allegiance to Caranthir.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §§173-174

claims.text: In , following the successful Quest of the Silmaril, new hope arose that Morgoth was not unconquerable, and the Union of Maedhros was formed. Among these preparations, the Men of Bór and of Ulfang were marshalled and trained for war, and given fair arms, and they summoned yet more of their kinsfolk out of the East. In spring of the following year, the Union made its first trial of strength, and soon succeeded in driving the Orcs out of Beleriand and reestablishing the frontiers as they had been during the Siege.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §212; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §213

claims.text:
Caranthir had the sobriquet of "the dark".
Caranthir's father-name was Morifinwë ("Dark Finwë"), for he was black-haired as his grandfather. The short form of this name was Moryo.
His mother-name was Carnistir ("Red-face") which was a compound of carnë and stîre.
In Ælfwine’s translation of the Quenta into Old English; Old English equivalents of Elvish names, his name is given as Colþegn Nihthelm and defined as "[Cranthir the Dark. O.E. col 'coal', þegn 'thane'; niht-helm lit. 'night-helm', but poetically referring to 'cover of night']"
An earlier variant of his name was Cranthir (N. "perfect"); it was alternatively spelled as Cranthor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of the Sons of Fëanor"; J.R.R. Tolkien, "From The Shibboleth of Fëanor" (edited by Carl F. Hostetter), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 41, July 2000, p. 10; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "III. The Quenta: Appendix 1: Fragments of a translation of The Quenta Noldorinwa into Old English, made by Ælfwine or Eriol; together with Old English equivalents of Elvish names"; J.R.R. Tolkien, "The Alphabet of Rúmil & Early Noldorin Fragments", in Parma Eldalamberon XIII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, Patrick H. Wynne, and Bill Welden), p. 161

claims.text:
In The Nauglafring, from the second volume of The History of Middle-earth, the only mention of Cranthor is the attack on Dior's realm to reclaim the Silmaril, and his subsequent death beside Celegorm.
In The Lay of the Children of Húrin, from the third volume, Flinding (Gwindor) tells Túrin about the Sons of Fëanor who live secretly in the forests of the East as unflinching foes of Morgoth, including "dark Cranthir".
In The Earliest 'Silmarillion', from the fourth volume, an early version has the Sons of Fëanor succeed in recovering the Silmaril after attacking Doriath and slaying Dior; however, owing to the curse of the gold, they then quarrelled for it, until only Maglor was left. This was very soon after emended to Elwing escaping with the Silmaril.
In The Earliest Annals of Beleriand, from the fourth volume, the sons of Ulfand (Uldor, Ulfast, and Ulwar) were most beloved by Cranthir among Sons of Fëanor, and they swore fealty to him. In the Battle of Unnumbered Tears, Uldor betrayed the Sons of Fëanor to Morgoth, and fell on their right flank. It was Cranthir who then slew Uldor.
In one version of the Battle of Sarn Athrad, the Dwarf army (likely of Nogrod) was defeated and "almost entirely destroyed by Caranthir".
While in the published Silmarillion Caranthir is recorded as the fourth son of Fëanor, in The Shibboleth of Fëanor Curufin is explicitly numbered as the fourth. This would then imply Caranthir to be the fifth son instead.
In The Nature of Middle-earth, a footnote regarding Finrod's epessë, Felegund, states that "This nick-name was probably actually given to Finrod not by Dwarves but by the Sons of Fëanor at least partly in derision. There was no great love between the Sons of Fëanor and the children of Finarphin, though they hid their enmity at need. (As when Curufin and Caranthir dwelt in the shelter of Nargothrond after the defeat of the Elves by Morgoth in the North). Moreover the Sons of Fëanor had much communication with the Dwarves of Nogrod and Belegost." It may be assumed that this was intended to refer to Celegorm instead.
